title: The rest of Avot
hook: year one read chapters one and two; now the rest, saying by saying
tomorrow: Akavia says look at three things and you won't sin. which three?

segments.voice: Year five opens in an upper room in Lod: study is greater, because study leads to deed. Read, then live. And yesterday left a question hanging about an old book.

Somewhere there's a show you stopped in season two, still waiting under continue watching. Year one of this path did that with a book. Pirkei Avot, the sayings of the fathers: the chain from Sinai, Hillel's if not now, when, Shammai's say little and do much, a skull floating on the water. Then chapter two ended, and the path moved on. So what's in the rest? Four more chapters, and this season reads them, one saying at a time.
screen: `STOPPED IN SEASON TWO.` → `AVOT, CHAPTERS ONE AND TWO.` → `WHAT'S IN THE REST?`

segments.voice: A quick walk down the hall, no spoilers past the doors. Each saying is a sentence or two: small enough to carry in a pocket, hard enough to argue over for a week. Chapter three opens with a sage named Akavia and three things to look at. Further on, Rabbi Akiva says every human being is beloved, because each was created in God's image. Before he speaks of any one people, he speaks of everyone. Chapter four has Ben Zoma's riddles. Who is rich? The one who is happy with their portion. Chapter five counts things in tens and sevens and fours, and keeps the arguments that last because they were for heaven's sake. And Ben Bag Bag says of the Torah: turn it, and turn it again, for everything is in it. Some sayings are gentle, some are hard, and a few will sound strange until a whole lesson opens them up. Now the review round, because the rest of Avot lands on what you already carry. You read a verse alone: bereshit bara. You said thanks in the root of Judah's name: todah. Letters count, and names matter. Judaism thinks and lives. And yesterday: read, then live. Avot is where those meet: short sayings, each one something to do. The rest of the sayings.

segments.voice: Here is how chapter three begins, in plain words: Akavia ben Mahalalel says, look at three things, and you won't come into the hands of sin. Say it once out loud, slowly, the way you'd read a line to a study partner across the table. Don't explain it yet; the three things are tomorrow's. For the rest of the sit, wonder which three you would have picked.

howItsDone: In Jewish custom Pirkei Avot is read on Shabbat afternoons in the summer months, a chapter a week, and it is printed in many prayer books; some read it with a study partner, saying by saying.

Pirkei Avot.meaning: chapters of the fathers: the sages' sayings

Akavia.meaning: Akavia ben Mahalalel, the sage who opens chapter three

Akiva.meaning: a sage of the Mishnah who calls every human beloved

Ben Zoma.meaning: a sage known in Avot for his riddles about wisdom and wealth

Ben Bag Bag.meaning: the sage who says: turn the Torah, and turn it again

Sinai.meaning: the mountain where, the Torah says, Moses received it

All Avot sayings paraphrased (after Taylor 1897, not on the validator's PD list): 3:1 Akavia's opening line only (the three things are day 1429); 3:14 Akiva, beloved is man for he was created in the image, then beloved are Israel; 4:1 Ben Zoma, who is wise (learns from every person) and who is rich (rejoices in his portion); 5:17 argument for heaven's sake; Ben Bag Bag, turn it and turn it for everything is in it (5:22 in many editions, 5:25/5:26 in others). Confirm paraphrases and numbering.

'Chapter five counts things in tens and sevens and fours' refers to the numbered sayings of Avot 5 (ten utterances, ten generations, seven traits of the clod and the wise, four types of people). Confirm.
Unity thread (light, on a review day): Avot 3:14 speaks of every human being created in God's image before it speaks of Israel; presented as the text's order, not as a claim about all traditions.
